X280.L4t: Full phosphocreatine resynthesis after very high intensity exercise takes about 4 minutes.
X280.L2f: Phosphocreatine is stored in muscle in quantities so large that it is rarely depleted during exercise, and it is rebuilt by anaerobic glycolysis alone.
X280.L3f: Phosphocreatine resynthesis is a direct and almost instantaneous chemical reversal that needs no mitochondrial involvement, so it is restored within seconds once exercise stops.
X280.L4f: Complete resynthesis of phosphocreatine after very high intensity exercise takes only about 10 seconds.

X271.L2t: Austin's command theory of law, set out in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined, was criticized by later legal theorists such as Hart for its simplistic picture of what laws are.
X271.L3t: Austin treats laws as observable facts, namely commands backed by sanctions that issue from a sovereign, and so overlooks the concepts and rules that give those facts their meaning as law.
X271.L4t: Austin is called a naive empiricist because he conceives of laws pragmatically, as observable commands and habits of obedience, instead of conceptually.
X271.L2f: Austin wrote his main jurisprudential work in the 1830s and based it on a detailed comparative survey of every legal system in the world at the time.
X271.L3f: Austin's view of law was modelled on a historical type of legal system that has since become obsolete, so it no longer fits how modern legal systems work.
X271.L4f: Austin is called a naive empiricist because his account of law rests on an anachronistic model of a legal system.
X271.cand_true: He conceives of laws pragmatically rather than conceptually
X271.cand_wrong1: His account of law rests on an anachronistic model of a legal system
X271.cand_wrong2: He denies any link between law and morality

X295.L2t: Friedrich Carl von Savigny, a leading figure of the German Historical School, argued against codifying German law in the early 1800s.
X295.L3t: For Savigny, law grows organically out of a people's shared spirit and customs, not out of any legislator's decree, so a theory that makes law a product of a sovereign's command contradicts the Volksgeist.
X295.L4t: The least likely statement is that law is the deliberate expression of a sovereign's will, since Savigny held that law arises from the people's spirit rather than from commands.
X295.L2f: Savigny's concept of the Volksgeist was developed in the 1830s as a response to Hegel's philosophy of the state and to the French Revolution.
X295.L3f: For Savigny, a people's spirit is too uniform and abstract to shape the particular rules of its law, so legal rules are tied to cultural character only in a loose and incidental way.
X295.L4f: The least likely statement is that a society's law is a reflection of its culture, since Savigny's Volksgeist denies any link between law and a people's culture.
X295.cand_true: Law is the deliberate expression of a sovereign's will
X295.cand_wrong1: A society's law is a reflection of its culture
X295.cand_wrong2: Law develops gradually out of a people's customs and shared consciousness

X260.L2t: U.S. law is organized as a hierarchy in which higher sources of law override conflicting lower ones.
X260.L3t: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution the highest law, and a treaty or statute that conflicts with it is invalid, so the Constitution ranks above treaties and federal statutes.
X260.L4t: The hierarchy runs from the U.S. Constitution, to treaties and federal statutes, to executive agreements, and finally to state law.
X260.L2f: U.S. law is ranked by how recently each source was created, with the newest sources generally overriding older ones.
X260.L3f: Because treaties and federal statutes are made through ratification and legislative votes, they carry the highest authority, and the Constitution is a framework that they can override.
X260.L4f: The hierarchy places treaties and federal statutes first, then the U.S. Constitution, then executive agreements, and then state law.
X260.cand_true: U.S. Constitution, treaties and federal statutes, executive agreements, state law
X260.cand_wrong1: Treaties and federal statutes, U.S. Constitution, executive agreements, state law
X260.cand_wrong2: U.S. Constitution, state law, treaties and federal statutes, executive agreements

X299.L2t: Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence that can arise during replication or from environmental damage, and they are the source of genetic variation.
X299.L3t: Because the cell's DNA polymerase copies bases with occasional unavoidable mistakes even without any mutagen present, errors arise naturally at a small baseline frequency.
X299.L4t: Mutations are DNA errors that occur spontaneously at a low rate, for example through replication mistakes.
X299.L2f: Mutations are changes in DNA that only occur in cells of the immune system and are never passed on to offspring.
X299.L3f: Since any change to the DNA sequence disrupts the protein it encodes, every mutation interferes with normal function and lowers an organism's fitness.
X299.L4f: Mutations are DNA errors that are always harmful to the organism.
X299.cand_true: occur spontaneously at a low rate
X299.cand_wrong2: only occur when exposed to radiation

X238.L2t: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional gut disorder marked by recurrent abdominal pain with altered bowel habits and is often worsened by stress.
X238.L3t: The sympathetic supply to the gut comes from preganglionic fibers in the thoracolumbar spinal cord, which travel through the splanchnic nerves to the prevertebral ganglia.
X238.L4t: The sympathetic innervation of the viscera involved in irritable bowel syndrome originates from spinal cord levels T7-L2.
X238.L2f: Irritable bowel syndrome is caused by structural inflammation of the colon wall that shows up on routine colonoscopy biopsy.
X238.L3f: The sympathetic supply to the lower gut comes from the lumbosacral cord, with fibers arising from the lower lumbar and upper sacral segments to reach the colon.
X238.L4f: The sympathetic innervation of the viscera involved in this patient's condition originates from L3-L5.

X240.L2t: An easement created by express grant and recorded is an interest in land that can later be terminated by operation of law, such as merger, release, or abandonment.
X240.L3t: When one person comes to own both the dominant and servient parcels, the easement is extinguished by merger, and a later conveyance of only the dominant parcel does not revive it unless a new easement is granted.
X240.L4t: The man should prevail because when the woman conveyed the house to him he owned both parcels, which extinguished the easement by merger, and his later deed to the purchaser did not create a new one.
X240.L2f: Express easements that are granted in writing and recorded generally stay in force for as long as the document says and are rarely affected by later changes in who owns the land.
X240.L3f: An easement appurtenant that was properly recorded passes automatically with the dominant parcel to every later owner, and it survives even if the same person briefly owns both parcels, so the man's deed carried it along.
X240.L4f: The purchaser should prevail because his warranty deed from the man carried the recorded easement with the house, so the man cannot block the path.
X240.cand_true: The man, because the easement was extinguished by merger
X240.cand_wrong1: The purchaser, because the warranty deed conveyed the easement
X240.cand_wrong2: The purchaser, because the recorded, marked path gave him an implied easement or notice

X246.L2t: The statement comes from a 20th-century British political scientist and economist associated with the London School of Economics.
X246.L3t: The remark was made by Harold Laski, the Fabian socialist and LSE professor who wrote A Grammar of Politics and wrote on law and the state.
X246.L4t: The statement that jurisprudence is the eye of law is attributed to Harold Laski.
X246.L2f: The statement comes from a 19th-century writer on early law and the evolution of legal institutions in ancient societies.
X246.L3f: The remark was made by the Victorian legal historian who wrote Ancient Law and traced the movement from status to contract.
X246.L4f: The statement that jurisprudence is the eye of law is attributed to Henry Maine.

X247.L2t: Bentham's felicific calculus proposed measuring pleasures and pains by dimensions such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent.
X247.L3t: The calculus requires summing the pleasures and pains of all the consequences of an act, including its far-reaching and unforeseeable effects, so its usability depends on whether those consequences can actually be known and totalled.
X247.L4t: The most powerful refutation is that it is impossible to calculate all the consequences of one's acts, so the calculus can never actually be carried out.
X247.L2f: Bentham developed the felicific calculus in his 1789 work as a way to compare the pleasures of different people, and critics have mostly targeted its claim that pleasures differ only in quantity.
X247.L3f: Because the calculus treats pleasure and pain as the basic units of value, the strongest objection would be one about whether pleasure and pain are an unavoidable part of every human life.
X247.L4f: The most powerful refutation is that pain and pleasure are inevitable features of life, which undermines the calculus.
X247.cand_true: It is impossible to calculate all the consequences of one's acts.
X247.cand_wrong1: Pain and pleasure are inevitable features of life.
X247.cand_wrong2: Pleasures differ in quality, not just quantity.

X250.L2t: Habermas's theory of law in Between Facts and Norms draws on his wider distinction between the system (state and economy) and the lifeworld (everyday communicative life).
X250.L3t: For Habermas, law as medium is the formal, general-rule steering mechanism that links to and controls the state and economy, whereas law as institution is anchored in the lifeworld's shared norms and values.
X250.L4t: Law as medium is formal, general rules that control the state and the economy, while law as institution lives in the lifeworld and gives shared values and norms an institutional form.
X250.L2f: Habermas wrote about law mainly in the 1920s, as part of an early Frankfurt School study of how newspapers and broadcasting shaped legal opinion.
X250.L3f: In Habermas's usage, 'medium' refers to mass communication channels such as press and broadcasting, and 'institution' refers to concrete bodies like courts that apply the law.
X250.L4f: Law as medium means the way law is portrayed by the media, and law as institution means the courts.
X250.cand_true: Medium: formal general rules controlling state and economy; institution: lifeworld-based shared norms and values
X250.cand_wrong1: Medium: law as presented by the media; institution: the courts
X250.cand_wrong2: Medium: law as written statutes; institution: law as enforced by the police and the executive

X239.L2t: Humans keep core body temperature near 37°C through thermoregulation, which is coordinated by the hypothalamus.
X239.L3t: In a hot environment the body cannot lose heat by radiation or conduction, so it relies on evaporative cooling, which means sweat is released from the skin and evaporates.
X239.L4t: The body compensates for higher environmental temperature by increasing the water it loses through the skin, as sweat evaporates and carries heat away.
X239.L2f: Thermoregulation is controlled mainly by the kidneys, which sense the temperature of the surrounding air and adjust the body's heat output.
X239.L3f: The main way the body gets rid of extra heat is by pumping blood faster through the body, so that more heat is carried away from the core.
X239.L4f: The body compensates for increased environmental temperature by increasing heart rate.

X303.L2t: Roe v. Wade (1973) was decided by the Supreme Court in a 7-2 vote and concerned a Texas statute that criminalized most abortions.
X303.L3t: The majority reasoned that the Fourteenth Amendment's protection of personal liberty includes a right to privacy broad enough to cover a woman's decision whether to end her pregnancy, so Texas's restriction intruded on that right.
X303.L4t: The decision is controversial because the majority held Texas's abortion law unconstitutional, finding that it violated a woman's constitutional right to privacy.
X303.L2f: Roe v. Wade was decided in the 1950s by a unanimous Supreme Court and involved a federal statute regulating medical practice.
X303.L3f: The justices in the majority ruled without reviewing any medical testimony, expert briefs, or scientific literature on pregnancy and fetal development, relying purely on legal argument.
X303.L4f: The decision is controversial because the Court failed to consider the medical evidence in reaching its ruling.
X303.cand_true: Texas abortion law held unconstitutional as violating a woman's right to privacy
X303.cand_wrong1: The Court failed to consider the medical evidence
X303.cand_wrong2: The Court allowed states to ban abortion entirely, giving the federal government no role

X245.L2t: Carbohydrate is the main fuel for high-intensity exercise, and muscle glycogen stores are limited and can be depleted by prolonged or intense effort.
X245.L3t: High-intensity exercise depends heavily on rapid glycolytic ATP production from carbohydrate, which fat oxidation cannot supply fast enough when carbohydrate availability is low.
X245.L4t: A low carbohydrate intake means lower glycogen and carbohydrate availability, so it may impair performance in high-intensity exercise.
X245.L2f: Dietary carbohydrate is stored in muscle mostly as triglyceride, and this store is rarely used during exercise of any intensity.
X245.L3f: When dietary carbohydrate is low, muscles compensate by increasing their glycogen breakdown rate to make up for the missing supply from the diet.
X245.L4f: A low carbohydrate intake results in greater reliance on muscle glycogen during exercise.
X245.cand_wrong1: Results in greater reliance on muscle glycogen during exercise
X245.cand_wrong2: Increases fat oxidation enough to improve high-intensity performance

X252.L2t: Hydrogen ions accumulate in muscle during high-intensity exercise and lower the pH of the muscle cells and blood.
X252.L3t: Hydrogen ions are a by-product of anaerobic glycolysis, where glucose is converted to pyruvate and then to lactate, so they appear when this pathway runs at a high rate.
X252.L4t: Hydrogen ions are formed when glycolysis is being used as a major means of resynthesising ATP.
X252.L2f: Hydrogen ions are produced in muscle mainly while the body is at complete rest and are cleared within seconds by the lungs.
X252.L3f: The breakdown of phosphocreatine to creatine and phosphate is the main energy reaction that releases hydrogen ions and acidifies the muscle.
X252.L4f: Hydrogen ions are formed when phosphocreatine breakdown occurs.
X252.cand_true: glycolysis is being used as a major means of resynthesising ATP
X252.cand_wrong2: aerobic oxidation of fats supplies most of the ATP

X226.L2t: The human hand is a highly versatile organ whose uses are often grouped into broad functional categories.
X226.L3t: The hand's main uses are classified by function, and these include gripping objects, striking things as in percussion, and gathering sensory information.
X226.L4t: Three of the five main uses of the hand are grip, percussion, and sensory perception.
X226.L2f: The hand is mostly valued for its fine skin sensitivity, which is why classifications of its uses stress perception over force.
X226.L3f: The main uses of the hand are classified by the kinds of tactile sensation it produces, so touching, feeling, and stroking are listed as core uses.
X226.L4f: Three of the five main uses of the hand are touch, feel, and stroke.

X344.L2t: In this puzzle Gus must sit immediately after Hana, and Ben must sit immediately after Cara, so each of those pairs occupies two adjacent slots.
X344.L3t: Since Dev is before Cara and Ben, Cara is before Hana, Ann and Ben are at least three slots apart, and exactly one person sits between Ann and Dev, Ann must be in slot 1 with Dev in slot 3, which leaves Ivo in slot 2.
X344.L4t: The schedule is Ann, Ivo, Dev, Cara, Ben, Elif, Hana, Gus, Finn in slots 1 to 9, with Dev in slot 3 and Ivo in slot 2.
X344.L2f: In this puzzle the pair Gus and Hana sits together in the middle of the order, and Ivo has to be placed beside Ann at the start of the schedule.
X344.L3f: Because exactly one person sits between Ann and Dev and Ivo must come early, Dev takes slot 2 directly after Ann, and Ivo then takes slot 3 right after him.
X344.L4f: The schedule has Dev in slot 2 and Ivo in slot 3, directly after Ann in slot 1.
X344.cand_true: Ann 1, Ivo 2, Dev 3, with Ivo in slot 2 and Dev in slot 3
X344.cand_wrong1: Dev in slot 2 and Ivo in slot 3
X344.cand_wrong2: Finn in slot 6 and Elif in slot 9

X330.L2t: Ben is placed immediately after Gus and Hana immediately after Ben, so the puzzle's constraints chain several of the nine people into fixed adjacent runs.
X330.L3t: Gus, Ben and Hana must sit in three consecutive slots in that order, and Ivo and Dev form another adjacent pair. Elif must come before Hana and at least three slots before Ben, while Cara sits exactly two slots from Ben.
X330.L4t: The schedule is Ann, Ivo, Dev, Elif, Cara, Gus, Ben, Hana, Finn in slots 1 to 9, so Elif is in slot 4 and Cara in slot 5.
X330.L2f: In puzzles like this, the person with no constraint pointing at them is always placed in the middle slot, so the most-constrained people end up at the ends.
X330.L3f: Because Cara must be two slots from Ben on the earlier side, Cara takes slot 4 right after the Ivo and Dev pair, and Elif follows in the next slot.
X330.L4f: Elif is in slot 5 and Cara is in slot 4, so the schedule has them in that order.
X330.cand_true: Elif in slot 4 and Cara in slot 5 (Ann, Ivo, Dev, Elif, Cara, Gus, Ben, Hana, Finn)
X330.cand_wrong1: Elif in slot 5 and Cara in slot 4
X330.cand_wrong2: Gus in slot 5 and Ben in slot 6

X353.L2t: Ann, Ben, Hana and Gus each have a required ordering relative to Ann, and Ben must come right after Ann.
X353.L3t: Cara and Elif must both come before Ann, while Ben (right after Ann), Hana and Gus all come after her, so Ann must be in slot 6, Ben in 7, Hana in 8 and Gus in 9.
X353.L4t: The schedule is Dev, Finn, Ivo, Cara, Elif, Ann, Ben, Hana, Gus in slots 1 through 9.
X353.L2f: In this kind of scheduling puzzle the 'at least three apart' rules usually apply only to people sitting in the middle slots, and the ordering rules rarely fix anyone's exact slot.

X321.L2t: Cara and Ann occupy adjacent slots with Cara first, and Elif and Gus must both come before Ann, so the early slots fill up quickly.
X321.L3t: Dev has to be at least three slots after Cara and before both Ben and Hana, which forces Dev into slot 7, and then Finn in slot 6 with exactly one person between Finn and Ben puts Ben in slot 8.
X321.L4t: The schedule is Elif, Gus, Cara, Ann, Ivo, Finn, Dev, Ben, Hana in slots 1 through 9, with Ben in slot 8 and Hana in slot 9.
X321.L2f: Most scheduling puzzles of this kind are solved by placing whoever has the most 'before' constraints in the final slot, and Hana usually ends up in a middle slot here.
X321.L3f: Because Dev and Ivo both come before Ben and Ben is far from Ann, Ben must come after Hana as well, which makes Ben the last person in slot 9.

X352.L2t: The ordering clues around Hana, Finn and Ivo place Hana early, and Ivo must come after Elif, Cara and Hana.
X352.L3t: Finn must be immediately before Hana, and Ann, Gus and Ivo all come after Hana. The Ben–Elif and Gus–Ivo gap clues then fix the rest of the later slots.
X352.L4t: The schedule is Finn, Hana, Elif, Dev, Ben, Cara, Gus, Ann, Ivo in slots 1 to 9.

X346.L4t: The schedule is Ann, Hana, Ivo, Ben, Cara, Gus, Dev, Finn, Elif in slots 1 through 9, so Cara is in slot 5.

X346.L3f: Only Ann, Hana and Ivo must come before Cara, and they fill slots 1 to 3, so Cara takes the very next open slot.
X346.L4f: Cara is in slot 4, directly after Ann, Hana and Ivo, with Gus in slot 5 right behind her.

X346.cand_wrong1: Cara in slot 4 right after Ann, Hana and Ivo

X351.L4f: Cara is in slot 8 and Hana is in slot 9, with the other seven people placed around them.

X329.L4t: The schedule is Hana, Finn, Cara, Ben, Ann, Gus, Elif, Ivo, Dev in slots 1 to 9, with Hana first and Dev last.

X361.L2t: Ivo, Finn and Gus are tied together by the "immediately after" clues, so they form one consecutive run of three slots.
X361.L3t: Dev comes before Cara, Cara before Hana and Ivo, and Ivo, Finn and Gus are consecutive, so Dev must be first and Cara early, which leaves Ann as the one person who can sit with a single gap between her and Cara.
X361.L4t: Dev is first, then Cara, Hana, Ann, Ben, Ivo, Finn, Gus, with Elif last in slot 9.
X361.L2f: In puzzles like this, the "immediately after" clues are usually decoys, and the gap clues alone fix the whole order.
